lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Wireless headphones use their own codecs' is stated as an absolute. Many headphones also use general music codecs, and the 'own' codecs are only built for low delay and low power some of the time. Scope 4: the multichannel and downmix group gets no space at all. That group includes Multichannel audio coding, Audio coding mode, Channel element, Channel pair element, Coupled channel, Lo/Ro and Lt/Rt downmix, Intensity stereo, Joint stereo and the interchannel cues, which is about 12% of the 109 terms. Only stereo appears, through parametric stereo. Flow 4: the wireless headphone sentence at the end of paragraph 4 does not grow from the low-data-rate stereo and high-frequency idea. It is a side note, and paragraph 5 does not pick it up. Clarity 4: paragraph 3 is the densest in the lesson. In nine sentences it introduces the filter bank, rounding, the scalefactor, blocks and pre-echo, and a beginner has to hold all of them at once. Language 4: 'coarsely' (used twice) is an uncommon word. 'describe some parts of the sound instead of coding them in full' and 'fill lost data with a likely sound' are vague when read literally.
lessons.comment: A strong, accurate lesson that follows the chain well: why codecs exist, how hearing-based coding works, the low-rate tricks, speech codecs, standards and frames, lossless coding and quality scores. Every named term matches its glossary plain English (checked on the base tables: perceptual audio coding, scalefactor, pre-echo, parametric stereo, code-excited linear prediction, audio frame, synchronization word, filter bank, bandwidth extension). The check script passes with 0 fails and 0 warns at 478 words, 8 paragraphs and an average sentence of 12.6 words. At 478 words there is almost no room left, so any addition needs a cut elsewhere. Weighted score is 4.2 (B). To reach 4.5 or higher, three changes would do it: rework the headphone sentence, which fixes accuracy and flow; add one sentence on multichannel coding, which fixes scope; and split or plain the wording in paragraph 3, which fixes clarity and language.

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the topic has 333 live terms. The lesson covers band shapes, Q and slope, parametric and graphic units, filter designs, phase, dynamic EQ, uses and measurement. Two things are missing. Notch and band-pass are not covered, even though the Welcome text names notches. How nearby bands interact is also missing. Filter designs (paragraph 4) take a lot of space, while the large corrective/creative/masking/spectral group gets only three sentences. Flow 4: paragraph 4 switches from filter designs to the timing of equalizers with no linking sentence. Paragraph 7 ('Some equalizers measure the sound first') is not linked to paragraph 6 and could be moved without loss. Clarity 3: paragraph 4 is six abstract sentences about filter responses and phase ('keeps the frequencies in step', 'shift some frequencies slightly later'), with no example a beginner can hold on to. The lesson also names about 12 terms (bands, bell, low shelf, high shelf, filter, Q, slope, parametric, graphic, dynamic equalization, room correction, pink noise), well above the standard's 2–6. Language 4: 'ring or smear' is figurative and vague, 'in step' is idiomatic, and 'The cost is' is a mild figure of speech. Glossary 4: 'A filter strongly reduces everything above or below a chosen frequency' is narrower than the glossary's Filter entry, which also covers band-pass and notch. The lesson calls the frequency parts 'bands', while the glossary's 'Band (EQ)' is a section of the equalizer that works on its own part of the range. Opening/closing 4: the opening (bass and treble knobs, ending on a question) is good. The closing brings in 'separate equalization of the middle and the sides of a stereo sound' in wording a beginner cannot picture. House rules 4: the check script passes with 0 fails and 0 warnings, but the script counts 7 'called' terms, above the standard's 2–6, and the lesson is at 479 words, the top of the range, which leaves no room for fixes.
lessons.comment: The lesson is accurate and checked against the glossary: Bessel, Butterworth, Chebyshev, linear-phase, minimum-phase, dynamic EQ, match EQ and room correction all agree with their plain English. The opening and the shapes-then-width chain work well. The main weakness is paragraph 4: it is dense and abstract, and it mixes filter designs with equalizer timing. The lesson also names too many terms. Rewriting paragraph 4 shorter also makes room for notch/band-pass and band interaction while staying under 480 words. Weighted score (15+8+8+6+8+4+4+4)/14 = 4.1 (B). Run the check script again after the fixes, because the word budget is tight.
lessons.fixes: CLARITY/LANGUAGE/FLOW (paragraph 4, replace the whole paragraph, about 18 fewer words): "Filters also differ in how they treat the sounds they keep. One design keeps the frequencies it lets through at the same level. Others are steeper, but the level of the frequencies they keep rises and falls slightly. Another keeps the frequencies in step, so sharp sounds do not ring or smear. Its slope is more gradual. Most equalizers shift some frequencies slightly later than others. One kind delays every frequency by the same amount. The cost is extra delay and sometimes a faint sound just before a sharp hit." -> "Filters also differ in what they do to the sound they keep. Some keep its level even. Some cut more steeply, but the kept level rises and falls slightly. Some keep all frequencies together in time, but cut more gradually. Most equalizers make some frequencies arrive slightly later than others. A linear-phase equalizer delays every frequency equally instead. The downside is extra delay and sometimes a faint sound just before a sudden hit." || SCOPE/GLOSSARY (Filter): "A filter strongly reduces everything above or below a chosen frequency." -> "A filter strongly reduces the frequencies above or below a chosen point, or in one narrow range." || SCOPE (band interaction, add after "A low Q changes a wide range."): add "Nearby bands also overlap, so their changes add together." || GLOSSARY (Band): "An equalizer works on chosen parts of the frequency range, called bands, and each band has a shape." -> "An equalizer is split into sections called bands.
